In the closing seconds of the Spurs' Oct. 30 loss to Houston, Johnson turned to Wembanyama for a potential game-tying basket. Amen Thompson had other ideas, stuffing Wembanyama's left-handed attempt at the rim. Asked afterward if he would have changed anything about his approach against the 6-foot-7 Thompson, Wembanyama answered in the affirmative. "I would have dunked," Wembanyama said. Behind the closed doors of the Spurs' practice facility, Wembanyama has been something of a mad scientist, tinkering with moves that have yet to unleash on an NBA court. For a star in search of a go-to move, the laboratory is always open. Utah coach Will Hardy was on the Spurs' development staff in the 2010s and saw firsthand the work Kawhi Leonard put into expanding the offensive repertoire that would eventually make him one of the game's most feared go-to scorers. "I don't think that the general fan has a full grasp of how long the road is before something becomes repeatable in a game," Hardy said. "I think you see things in workouts and then you see it in practice and then you see a few attempts here and there in a game, maybe with not as much success. "By the time something has become a go-to in a game, there is so much work that's gone before." Golden State coach Steve Kerr has had a front-row seat to some of the most accomplished closers in NBA history. He played alongside Duncan in San Antonio and Michael Jordan in Chicago. For the past 13 seasons, he has coached Stephen Curry with the Warriors. If anyone might know the secret to developing a go-to move, Kerr has seen a few different versions of the process. He doesn't believe in a universal blueprint. "I think everybody's different," Kerr said. "You have to figure out your own game and what that means. You think of any great player in the league and they've all done it differently. They've all done it their own way. … Part of being a young, emerging player at that level is figuring out what that means for yourself." Even Wembanyama hones his own signature move, he is having little trouble laying waste to NBA defenses without one. Heading into Sunday afternoon's matinee at Utah, Wembanyama was averaging 28.8 points in his first 13 games, third most in the league. Since the Spurs' first trip to Salt Lake City on Oct. 30, he has piled up six games of at least 30 points, including a 40-point explosion and a career-best 52-point masterpiece against Dallas that also featured 24 rebounds and eight blocks. "He just does it from all three levels right now and then anytime he has a switch, they just literally throw the ball to the top of the backboard (for a dunk)," Suns coach Jordan Ott said. "When that starts, it's so deflating." In that, perhaps Wembanyama has already stumbled upon his signature move -- the self alley-oop. Spurs teammate De'Aaron Fox believes the right answer for Wembanyama might be something simpler. Wembanyama doesn't necessarily need to polish some amazing feat of footwork or invent a new way to finish at the rim, Fox said. He simply needs to put that Boeing-sized wingspan to work, rising up to shoot over defenders who have no realistic hope of bothering the shot. Think Abdul-Jabbar's skyhook, without the extra choreography. "The best players that have ever played the game all have a mid-range shot," Fox said. "When he can take the easy ones, then we start seeing all the spectacular plays come." Fox continued. "When he's making that (mid-range) shot, then his pump fake becomes even more lethal," he said. "Now he's one-dribble dunking the ball. I just think it opens up the game for himself and everyone else that's around him." Wembanyama promises something is coming. He can't yet say what or when. "It's always a challenge to balance the team goals because for every one of us, we're not there to work on our game -- we're here to win games," Wembanyama said. "So (a signature move) is not a top, top priority." For now, Wembanyama is still fine-tuning, still searching for the move that might one day become his calling card. The rest of the NBA hopes he takes his time. "If that's part of the progression," Kerr said, "then we're all in huge trouble." Subscribe There’s more to San Antonio with the Express-News. item.title: Drake Maye could miss rest of season after suffering lower leg injury, reports say
item.description: FILE - New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye (10) is sacked by Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson (97) during an NFL football game in Munich, Germany, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. (AP Photo/Lennart Preiss, File) Lennart Preiss The New England Patriots could be without quarterback Drake Maye for the rest of the season. Maye suffered a significant lower leg injury during Sunday’s game against the Lions in Germany, according to multiple reports. ESPN and NFL Network reported that Maye suffered a serious injury that could keep him sidelined for the remainder of the season. NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport reported Monday that a source described Maye’s injury as a “significant lower leg injury” that will keep him out for an extended period. Rapoport said Maye and the Patriots will seek additional medical information after returning to the United States. Maye was injured when he was sacked during the Patriots’ first drive of the game. He was initially considered questionable to return but was later ruled out. Before the Patriots left Germany, head coach Mike Vrabel said Maye was unable to continue playing. “He couldn’t, couldn’t function, couldn’t play, couldn’t run, couldn’t do whatever he needed to do to play quarterback, to protect himself, to execute or function at that level,” Vrabel said. “I know that it was a lower leg injury. I don’t know the exact details of it, but I know he couldn’t go back in.” The Patriots have a bye this week before facing the Chargers in Los Angeles on Nov. 29. This is a developing story. item.title: ‘I heard’: Journalist shares what Bayern talked about Lennart Karl future
item.description: ‘I heard’: Journalist shares what Bayern talked about Lennart Karl future Bayern Munich youngster Lennart Karl is a special talent, but he recently faced public criticism from the club’s honorary president Uli Hoeneß. The 18-year-old made a breakthrough into the first-team under Vincent Kompany last season, and scored nine goals and registered eight assists across all competitions. He finished three places below Lamine Yamal in the Kopa Trophy (best young player), and has a bright future at Bayern. What Bayern think about Lennart Karl View this post on Instagram While many people acknowledged the Bayern winger’s drop in form, there were others who were unhappy that such thoughts have been made public. Christian Falk has exclusively told CFBayern Insider that Bayern are happy with the player’s development, but handing him a new contract is not currently on the agenda. The club are waiting to see what Michael Olise decides about his future, and once his situation is sorted, there will be more clarity on Karl. The Bild journalist said : “Lennart Karl is a very special person at 18 years of age. As journalists, we often say everything is really quiet and really boring when it comes to interviewing players these days because everyone is so media-trained and giving the same answers. Lennart Karl is not like that, and he doesn’t play like that either. He also doesn’t wear clothes like that! He was at the Ballon d’Or ceremony, having finished three places below Lamine Yamal in the Kopa Trophy (best young player). He has a big future in the sport, which other clubs are no doubt aware of, and certainly Bayern are wary of the wandering gaze from their European rivals. “I heard there was an internal meeting where Bayern talked with the Lennart Karl side. They told him that he’s a very important player for Bayern Munich and that they’re very happy with his development. But they weren’t so happy that they were prepared to talk about a new contract! He’s still earning a salary of about €2.5m gross [£2.08m]. So, you see, there’s a lot of space there to work with in future. Everyone is now waiting for a decision from Michael Olise. When this decision is made, everyone will be able to see things more clearly around Lennart Karl and his future at Bayern Munich.” Lennart Karl needs to step up with key players injured (Photo by Mateo Villalba Sanchez/Getty Images) This is an important season for Karl, and he can shut down his critics with strong performances. Michael Ballack, the player’s agent, certainly was not happy with the comments directed at the youngster. Karl has registered three goals and two assists across all competitions this season, and he will be aiming to improve the numbers. With Ismael Saibari and Serge Gnabry currently out injured, Karl is expected to feature heavily after the November international break.

item.title: Versatile Barcelona defender still absent from group training as key midfielder makes progress ahead of Villarreal clash
item.description: Versatile Barcelona defender still absent from group training as key midfielder makes progress ahead of Villarreal clash Barcelona have yet to welcome Jules Kounde back to full team training, leaving Hansi Flick with another fitness concern ahead of Sunday’s La Liga meeting with Villarreal on November 22. According to SPORT , the French defender was still working separately when the squad resumed training on Monday, November 16, despite hopes that the international break would give him enough time to recover from his left ankle sprain. It is to be noted that Kounde has now spent a month recovering from the injury sustained against Real Betis on October 17. What initially appeared to be a relatively minor setback has developed into a longer absence , with persistent discomfort preventing the defender from returning to normal training. Jules Kounde is still not training with the group. (Photo by Eric Alonso/Getty Images) On the other hand, however, there is more encouraging news concerning Dani Olmo, although Barcelona will also need to assess his response to training before confirming his availability against Villarreal. Kounde’s recovery takes longer than Barcelona expected Barcelona initially anticipated that Kounde would miss approximately a week after spraining his left ankle against Betis. However, the defender continued experiencing discomfort even after the initial inflammation subsided, which complicated his recovery. The international break offered an opportunity to complete his rehabilitation without the demands of competitive matches, but his continued absence from group training suggests that the final stage of recovery has proved more difficult than expected. Dani Olmo provides a boost after recovery Barcelona are hoping Dani Olmo could return from his injury against Villarreal. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images) Olmo’s situation offers a more positive development for Flick, as the midfielder has been working towards a return after suffering a grade-one tear in his left adductor during Barcelona’s Champions League meeting with Paris Saint-Germain. It must be remembered that his initial recovery estimate was approximately one month. His progress has been encouraging, with Barcelona targeting the Villarreal fixture for his return . However, a lot still depends on progressing through rehabilitation and eventually receiving medical clearance, mostly becuase has still has not completed a full group training session yet.

The 26-year-old winger has endured a difficult start to the 2026/27 campaign under Jose Mourinho, managing a paltry return of just one goal and three assists in 12 appearances. I had the habit of playing friendlies as if they were just another club game, and it took me a while to understand that, with Brazil, friendlies are like a World Cup,” he said. “The fans don’t care if it’s a friendly. I have to go out there, score goals, and make the team win.” Ready to step up. (Photo by Koji Watanabe/Getty Images) Vinicius added that he had previously approached international duty with the wrong mindset, but that had changed now. “Before, I used to come here to enjoy the moment with my friends and end up disconnecting too much. item.title: Canada issues update on Alphonso Davies injury
item.description: Photo by Getty Images | Getty Images Bayern Munich star Alphonso Davies started his first Canada match in a long time on Friday against Guatemala, captaining the side and hoping that he would be able to last a full 90 minutes on the field for his na tional team for the first time in around two years. It was not to be, however, as after just 5 minutes he slipped in an attempt to block a shot and quickly signaled that he could not continue. Despite Davies’ later proclamation that he could have theoretically stayed on the field, doing so was deemed an unnecessary risk, and he was taken off immediately . item.description: Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers suffered a brutal loss to the Cincinnati Bengals, and the all-time great QB had far from an all-time great performance. Hopefully, Rodgers can turn his form around in the next game and see out his final season in the NFL in the best way possible. item.title: 'Not competitive' Brazil can improve, insists Ancelotti
item.description: Carlo Ancelotti faced criticism in Brazil after the Selecao lost 3-2 to Japan (Roslan RAHMAN) Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti on Monday promised an improved performance in the year-ending clash against Singapore, admitting that his squad was "currently not competitive." The Selecao lost 3-2 against Japan in a friendly in Singapore on Saturday, where Ancelotti and skipper Raphinha were red-carded after Japan scored the dramatic clincher in stoppage time. "Given that the team is currently not competitive, I want to do more," Ancelotti told reporters in Singapore, where Brazil play on Tuesday. The Italian, Brazil's first-ever permanent foreign coach, said: "I want to do more because I enjoy being here, so that the team can become more competitive on the global stage. "The priority is to play well first (tomorrow) and to do well." Ancelotti, 67, is coming under increasing pressure, following a string of underwhelming performances including two defeats, two wins and a draw in Brazil's last five international outings. Japan avenged a 2-1 defeat by Brazil in their previous meeting at this year's World Cup, when the South Americans beat them in a round-of-32 clash. After Saturday's loss, Ancelotti faced a barrage of criticism, including from former Brazilian national team star Romario. Ancelotti brushed off Romario's remarks, saying "like anyone he has the right to express an opinion." But the former Real Madrid coach, who reacted with fury after Brazil appealed for a foul in the build-up to Japan's winning goal on Saturday -- which was upheld by VAR -- said that his team "didn't deserve to lose" against Japan. Japan face Paraguay on Tuesday in the second match of the double-header at Singapore's National Stadium. str-jhe/gj

item.title: YouTube Gold: When There Was No Dunk
item.description: American varsity basketball player Lew Alcindor (later known as Kareem Abdul-Jabbar) of UCLA during a game against University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, 1967. (Photo by PhotoQuest/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s probably very hard for fans today to understand how dominant Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, then known as Lew Alcindor, was when he was at UCLA. First of all, though freshmen weren’t eligible, almost everyone stayed for four years. For the three years he was on the varsity, Kareem won three national championships and led UCLA to an 88-2 record over those three years. And in one of those games, against Elvin Hayes and Houston, he had an eye injury. He was so dominant, in fact, that the NCAA did something they’ve only rarely done: they changed the rules because of a specific player. Like Bill Russell, whose dominance led to the goaltending rule, and Wilt Chamberlain, who forced the NCAA to widen the lane and to require that foul shots be taken from behind the line. (Chamberlain had a habit of taking off from behind the foul line and dunking), the NCAA made a major rule change for Kareem: they outlawed the dunk. They cited other reasons, but everyone knew. However, the rule backfired in a big way: deprived of the easiest shot for an athletic big man who was vastly more talented than his opponents, Kareem began to practice the Mikan Drill relentlessly (the Mikan drill, named for George Mikan, is where you do a left-handed hook shot, then one with the right). Ultimately, this evolved into the single-most deadly shot in the history of the game and, quite possibly, the most devastating single offensive weapon in the history of sports. The rule was finally repealed in time for the 1976-77 season. During those years, fans missed seeing not just Kareem dunk, but also players as great as Julius Erving and David Thompson. item.description: Carlos Alcaraz. © Imagn Carlos Alcaraz’s loyal fans have openly criticized Andy Murray’s brother, Jamie, for taking a swipe at the Spaniard’s entourage. Jamie, a doubles specialist in his playing days, took a dig at the size of Alcaraz’s entourage, wondering why the former World No. 1 Spaniard needs so many people to travel with him. Currently, Alcaraz is in Turin for the year-end ATP Finals. Jamie is covering the prestigious event as a pundit for Sky Sports Tennis. Here, the former men’s doubles World No. 1 said : “Obviously over the years, it’s been a thing about having the physio, the strength conditioning trainer, the agent, the nutritionist, the doctor, all that stuff and it’s packed right? It’s packed. For me, it’s too much. You see Alcaraz in the gym before the match and there’s six people standing around just watching him on a foam roller. What world are we living in?” Several Alcaraz fans objected to what Jamie said and took to X (formerly Twitter) to criticize the Brit. One fan wrote: (translated from Spanish via Grok) “This is just criticizing for the sake of criticizing now. Clearly, Andy Murray is much smarter and more elegant than his brother.” Carlos Alcaraz to get ATP Finals campaign underway with Round Robin phase clash against Frances Tiafoe Alcaraz is slated to lock horns with Frances Tiafoe of the USA in his first match at the 2026 ATP Finals. The Spaniard is the favorite on paper to win the prestigious year-end event this year given his rampant form in the buildup to the tournament, which included title triumphs in Tokyo, Vienna and the Paris Masters. However, Alcaraz has never won the ATP Finals, and the closest he came was last year, when he fell to Jannik Sinner in the final. Against Tiafoe, the Spaniard should be confident but cautious. Alcaraz leads the head-to-head 2-1 , with the American’s only win in the rivalry having come way back in 2021 at the Barcelona Open. However, their subsequent matches were five-set thrillers, with Alcaraz narrowly edging their 2022 US Open and 2024 Wimbledon clashes. item.title: Belgium's Lukaku retires from international football
item.description: Romelu Lukaku made his Belgium debut in 2010 (JOHN THYS) Belgium forward Romelu Lukaku on Monday retired from international football after scoring 94 goals in 135 games for his country, saying he was "at peace" with his decision. Lukaku featured in four World Cups for the Red Devils and helped them reach the quarter-finals of this year's tournament before losing to eventual winners Spain. The 33-year-old, who now plays for Turkish club Fenerbahce, made his debut in 2010 as a teenager and was an unused substitute in Sunday's 4-1 Nations League win over Italy. "These 16 years I gave all I had for the national team. It was a nice ride and I enjoyed every single moment," Belgium's record goal scorer said on Instagram. "To the Belgium fans, thank you for the support you gave our team. I am proud to have represented my country in 4 World Cups and 3 European Championships. "I will never forget those moments. I'm at peace with my decision to stop here," Lukaku said. The former Chelsea, Manchester United and Inter Milan forward was part of Belgium's so-called 'golden generation'. Lukaku, alongside Kevin De Bruyne, Thibaut Courtois and Eden Hazard, finished third at the 2018 World Cup, a best-ever finish for Belgium in the tournament but they failed to lift a trophy during the period. "I played with amazing teammates that I will always be grateful for," Lukaku said. "I want to thank them all. I want to thank all the coaches as well for pushing and trusting me to help the team," he added. - 'Legend, my brother' - A host of fellow Belgian players paid tribute to Lukaku. "Legend, my brother," midfielder Axel Witsel said on Instagram. "Thank you for everything my bro," Courtois said. "So many amazing memories," the Real Madrid goalkeeper added. Lukaku's last appearance for his country came in October's 4-1 loss to France. "Beyond his exceptional performances on the pitch, he has been a true leader, with a strong personality and an essential role in the dressing room," Lukaku's former team-mate and now Belgium's technical director Simon Mignolet said in a statement from the Belgian football association. "We respect his decision and are deeply grateful to him for everything he has brought to our national team," the former Liverpool goalkeeper added. Belgium's first game without Lukaku will be a Nations League last-eight fixture in March. "We must now turn our attention to the future and prepare for the Nations League quarter-finals," Mignolet said. "With the ambition of continuing to make progress as a team," he added. mad/ec/iwd/gj

item.description: The Cape and Islands high school football player polls concluded with Barnstable’s Isaiah Chisholm earning the final honor and Dennis-Yarmouth’s Grayden Campbell finishing as the season’s only three-time winner. Chisholm closed out the voting with his first poll victory after helping the Red Hawks earn a late-season win. Campbell separated himself from the field with three victories, earning recognition multiple times for his performances at quarterback for the Dolphins. Stroud to cool off Texans quarterback's fast start The backs-against-the-wall routines Berry and Watson are miraculously pulling off have permeated the entire locker room. “Whenever you have in your head that you can come back and win this game … and you have all the confidence in the world, those are the scariest teams,” said backup safety Donovan McMillon, who made the game-clinching pass breakup with one second remaining on a deep jump ball Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud intended for wide receiver Nico Collins. Against the Texans, the Browns had their fifth-biggest comeback in franchise history and the largest since Oct. 5, 2014, when they rallied from a 25-point deficit to beat the Tennessee Titans. Their four double-digit comeback wins are the most in the NFL in 2026 and the most in any Browns season. Cleveland is also the first team in league history whose first six wins of a season have all come by four points or fewer, according to ESPN. The Browns fell behind 17-0 when Stroud connected with wide receiver Xavier Hutchinson for an 11-yard touchdown pass with 11:21 left in the second quarter. What were our instant thoughts? Berry has added those players and many others who have ascended. Watson is clicking with the offense’s young playmakers when it matters most. “Seeing who's the right guys, who's not the right guys, I think it's just an ongoing process,” Browns cornerback Denzel Ward said. “And everybody’s done a great job of getting the right guys in here, the right coaches, and I think we just all kind of meshed very well.” As hard as it is to believe, Berry and Watson have their fingerprints all over a cohesive operation squarely in the playoff picture through Week 10. There was likely a lot of angst and tension in the building for weeks as the Nittany Lions tried to end their four-game losing streak, but all of those feelings should be gone now. With mostly everything trending in the right direction for them, let’s look at the biggest storylines they are dealing with this week. Man down Running back Carson Hansen had his best game of the season against Washington — and then he proceeded to one-up himself on Saturday against the Golden Gophers . Nobody knows the extent of the injury yet, but hopefully it isn’t anything too serious. Unlikely outcome Penn State’s chances of making a Bowl Game were murky at best after a four-game losing streak to begin Big Ten play. But after a three-game winning streak to make their record 6-4, the Nittany Lions will likely be playing football next month. While they could potentially earn a trip without another win this season, taking one of these last two games would be helpful to securing a more prestigious Bowl Game. It’s important for Penn State to impress as many people as possible down the stretch in hopes of beginning the 2027 season as a ranked team. Boredom breeds creativity Penn State will be going up against a couple of teams near the bottom of the Big Ten — Rutgers and Maryland — in the final two games of the season. With a Bowl Game appearance all but locked up, the coaching staff could look to experiment since they have some room for error. They can use these last two games to test out new personnel groupings, trick plays, and they can even try to get some guys on the field who haven’t played much this year. The Nittany Lions should win at least one of these games handily, so they would be wise to look for some more advantages. Final countdown This Penn State team is going to look a lot different next season. There are a lot of players in their final year of eligibility, like quarterback Rocco Becht , and some going to the NFL, like linebacker Tony Rojas . There are too many players to list all of them, but they have made tremendous contributions to this year’s team that will need to be replaced next season. Watch all of those players closely, because they’ll likely be playing inspired football as their collegiate careers wind down. Déjà vu It may not seem like it, but this season has unfolded almost exactly like 2025. Although the midseason losing streaks were different lengths, both teams had impressive starts and brutal rough patches in the middle of the season. Now, this iteration of Nittany Lions has a chance to end the season on an extended winning streak like that team did. The 2025 roster won its final three regular season games and then beat Clemson in the Pinstripe Bowl. Hopefully next year’s team doesn’t have any plans to recreate these scripts because they could make the College Football Playoff if they cut out the long losing streaks. item.title: ‘We all fell in love with him’ – Hull coach shares what Lewis Koumas was like behind the scenes
item.description: ‘We all fell in love with him’ – Hull coach shares what Lewis Koumas was like behind the scenes A member of the coaching staff at Hull City has spoken very highly of what Lewis Koumas was like behind the scenes during his loan move at the MKM Stadium. The Liverpool striker spent the second half of last season with the Tigers, playing a part in their promotion to the Premier League with three goals in 18 Championship appearances (including the play-offs). He’s since become a fixed first-team player at Anfield, being handed five starts among his 14 appearances across all competitions and scoring in the Champions League victory over LASK in October. Everyone at Hull ‘fell in love with’ Koumas Hull assistant coach Dean Holden spoke to The Redmen TV about how Koumas immediately won people over with his humility and hardworking attitude. The 47-year-old said: “Within a week, everyone fell in love with him, from Stan on the door, the security guy, to the kitchen staff, kit men, the lot. We all fell in love with him. “You know why? Just because he’s a real humble lad who just wants to be the best he can be and affects people around him in an energetic manner and just loves football.” Holden went on to share anecdotes of Koumas being out on the training pitch along with Joe Gelhardt ’20 minutes out before everyone else is in the gym’, telling coaches not to ‘sugarcoat’ advice to him, and waiting patiently for his mother to collect him after he scored a late winner for Hull on his debut against Blackburn instead of ‘going out on the town and celebrating’. (Photo by Alex Pantling/Getty Images) Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust Koumas appears to have a sky-high ceiling While we’re sure that the Liverpool youngster has been helped by sage advice from his father Jason, who graced the Premier League with West Brom and Wigan, the onus is still on him to put all of that bequeathed wisdom into action, and he’s most certainly doing that. Andoni Iraola clearly has plenty of faith in the 21-year-old if he’s playing him regularly, even starting him against Manchester City (albeit that Alexander Isak wasn’t fit), and the young striker is repaying that trust with his performances on the pitch. John Aldridge voiced his belief that the Wales international will ‘ play for Liverpool for a long time ‘, with Koumas standing out for his indefatigable pressing in the final third, which carries echoes of the beloved Bobby Firmino. The stories shared by Holden testify to the tremendous attitude of the Reds youngster, who’s remained grounded and earned his place in the first-team squad to the extent that he’s nudged Federico Chiesa further down the pecking order. We’re sure there’s still so much more to come from the Welshman, provided he can maintain the traits which have taken him this far already and (fingers crossed) avoid any major injury issues.

item.title: Kentucky vs. Missouri game glance, opening odds, and early prediction
item.description: Nine days ago, Kentucky Football was in the College Football Playoff conversation. Now, the Wildcats are trying to save a season that was turning into something special. The 21-14 loss to Florida on Saturday night at Kroger Field hurt more than most. Kentucky came in as a three-point favorite at home against a 5-4 Gators team. The Cats took a 7-2 lead into halftime and still led 14-13 going into the fourth quarter. Then Florida took over. Aaron Philo ran for 102 yards, the Gators ran for 211 as a team, and Kentucky managed just 61 rushing yards on 27 carries. That’s a season low for a team that came in averaging almost 164 per game. Will Stein didn’t sugarcoat it afterward. He said his team came up short in all three phases. That one stings because of how good this season had been. This was the team that went to College Station and beat No. 9 Texas A&M by 10. It came back from 17 down to win in overtime at South Carolina, beat No. 10 LSU 35-34 in overtime and sent the fans onto the field, then won in Norman. Kentucky was 7-1 and ranked in the top ten of the CFP rankings. Back-to-back losses to Tennessee and Florida later, the playoff dream is just about gone. But there’s still a lot to play for. Kentucky is 7-3 and bowl eligible with two games left: at Missouri and Louisville at home. Win both, then win a bowl game, and Kentucky reaches 10 wins. The program has only done that four times in its history: 1950, 1977, 2018 and 2021. In Stein’s first year, against what his own players called a whole lot of doubt back in August, that would be a remarkable finish. It starts Saturday night in Columbia. Game Info Matchup: Kentucky (7-3) at Missouri (6-4, 3-4 SEC) When: Saturday, Nov. 21, 7:30 p.m. ET Where: Faurot Field at Memorial Stadium, Columbia, MO. TV: SEC Network Odds: Missouri -6.5, over/under 50.5 (FanDuel) All-time series: Kentucky leads 9-5 Last meeting: Missouri won 38-21 in Lexington in 2023 Opponent at a Glance: Missouri Tigers Head coach: Eli Drinkwitz (7th season) Missouri started the year ranked No. 25 in the preseason polls. For a while, it looked like the Tigers were exactly who people thought they were. They blew out Florida 45-17, held Texas A&M to six points in a 27-6 win and beat Arkansas by 24. The problem is what happened against good teams. Missouri lost at Mississippi State in September, lost 31-3 at Ole Miss, lost 34-20 at home to Texas and just got rolled 48-21 by No. 1 Georgia in Athens. Two straight losses ended the Tigers’ playoff hopes. The Georgia game was ugly from the first snap. Quarterback Austin Simmons threw an interception on the first play, Georgia scored two plays later, and Missouri was down 31 at halftime. Drinkwitz called it “not a good plan offensively or defensively,” and the Tigers went 2-for-11 on third down. Aaron Philo ran for 102 yards, the Gators ran for 211 as a team, and Kentucky managed just 61 rushing yards on 27 carries. That’s a season low for a team that came in averaging almost 164 per game. Will Stein didn’t sugarcoat it afterward. He said his team came up short in all three phases. That one stings because of how good this season had been. This was the team that went to College Station and beat No. 9 Texas A&M by 10. It came back from 17 down to win in overtime at South Carolina, beat No. 10 LSU 35-34 in overtime and sent the fans onto the field, then won in Norman. Kentucky was 7-1 and ranked in the top ten of the CFP rankings. Back-to-back losses to Tennessee and Florida later, the playoff dream is just about gone. But there’s still a lot to play for. Kentucky is 7-3 and bowl eligible with two games left: at Missouri and Louisville at home. Win both, then win a bowl game, and Kentucky reaches 10 wins. The program has only done that four times in its history: 1950, 1977, 2018 and 2021. In Stein’s first year, against what his own players called a whole lot of doubt back in August, that would be a remarkable finish. It starts Saturday night in Columbia. Game Info Matchup: Kentucky (7-3) at Missouri (6-4, 3-4 SEC) When: Saturday, Nov. 21, 7:30 p.m. ET Where: Faurot Field at Memorial Stadium, Columbia, MO. TV: SEC Network Odds: Missouri -6.5, over/under 50.5 (FanDuel) All-time series: Kentucky leads 9-5 Last meeting: Missouri won 38-21 in Lexington in 2023 Opponent at a Glance: Missouri Tigers Head coach: Eli Drinkwitz (7th season) Missouri started the year ranked No. 25 in the preseason polls. For a while, it looked like the Tigers were exactly who people thought they were. They blew out Florida 45-17, held Texas A&M to six points in a 27-6 win and beat Arkansas by 24. The problem is what happened against good teams. Missouri lost at Mississippi State in September, lost 31-3 at Ole Miss, lost 34-20 at home to Texas and just got rolled 48-21 by No. 1 Georgia in Athens. Two straight losses ended the Tigers’ playoff hopes. The Georgia game was ugly from the first snap. Quarterback Austin Simmons threw an interception on the first play, Georgia scored two plays later, and Missouri was down 31 at halftime. Drinkwitz called it “not a good plan offensively or defensively,” and the Tigers went 2-for-11 on third down. Missouri 2026 Results W 54-14 vs. Arkansas-Pine Bluff W 38-21 vs. Kansas W 27-17 vs. Troy L 31-24 at Mississippi State W 45-17 vs. Florida W 27-6 vs. Texas A&M L 31-3 at Ole Miss W 34-10 at Arkansas L 34-20 vs. Texas L 48-21 at Georgia Players to Know QB Austin Simmons: He won the job over Matt Zollers in the spring and opened the season 17 of 19 for 252 yards and four touchdowns. When he gets protection he can pick you apart. RB Ahmad Hardy: A preseason AP First Team All-American and the engine of the run game. Kentucky’s run defense has to be better than it was against Florida. RB Jamal Roberts: The second back in a deep backfield. WR Donovan Olugbode: Simmons’ favorite target and the guy they go to on third down. OL Cayden Green: A preseason Second Team All-American who anchors the line. Keys to the Game Fix the run defense. Florida ran 48 times for 211 yards and wore Kentucky down in the second half. Missouri will try the exact same thing with Hardy. If Kentucky can’t set the edge, it’s going to be a long night. Get the run game going again. Kentucky’s offense works when the run sets up Kenny Minchey. Sixty-one rushing yards won’t win in the SEC, let alone on the road at night. Attack the secondary. Pass defense has been Missouri’s weak spot all year. Georgia’s Gunner Stockton went 18 of 24 for 252 yards. Minchey needs to take his shots. Start fast. Missouri has started slow on the road and on the ropes. Kentucky has led into the second half against Alabama, Tennessee, and Florida and lost all three. The second half is where this team has to grow up. Win the turnover battle. Kentucky’s big wins this year came down to a play here and there. Simmons has been careless with the ball against good defenses. Make him pay. Our Early Prediction This one comes down to which team handles adversity better. Both are coming off back-to-back losses, and both had playoff hopes that are now gone. Missouri has the home field and is favored by almost a touchdown. Kentucky has the head coach who has won close games all year. What gives me some hope is the bounce back. After Alabama blew them out, the Cats went on the road and beat Texas A&M. Stein has had a whole week to get this team’s attention after being called out for not looking like themselves. I think Kentucky responds. It won’t be pretty, but the Cats grind out a road win and stay alive for a 10-win season.

item.title: Roma finalize permanent deal for Balerdi
item.description: Roma finalize permanent deal for Balerdi Leonardo Balerdi has quickly become an important player for Gian Piero Gasperini. Upon his arrival, the Grugliasco-born coach called him one of the new captains, given that he wore the captain’s armband at Marseille. Born in 1999, the defender arrived on loan from OM, and the buyout is contingent on the defender’s appearances. To trigger the €11 million obligation, Balerdi will have to play 40% of the matches. The figure increases if he makes more appearances: €14 million, with over 55% of matches lasting at least 45 minutes. The former Marseille player could be satisfied with just 20% of the matches in the second half of the season. In this case, Roma would have to pay the French club €9 million. Gasperini considers him an important player, and in a short time, he’s carved out a significant niche for himself, considering the starting lineup alongside Mancini, Ndicka, and Hermoso: 639 minutes, highlighted by a brace away to Napoli. As La Gazzetta dello Sport reports, if an automatic buyout were to arrive, all the conditions are in place for this to happen: the Giallorossi club and the player are already in full agreement regarding the contract renewal. In fact, the parties have already put everything down in black and white. The desire of all is to continue together.

item.title: Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe
item.description: Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: s omehow, anyhow . What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too. Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch. Continue reading...

item.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
item.description: Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can When you walk up from Haydons Road railway station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium. AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter – but that makes running a loss‑making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board, which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.” Continue reading...

item.title: Portugal did the extraordinary with Cristiano Ronaldo. Can they do it without him?
item.description: The captain, the talisman, the brand: former teammates and experts discuss Portugal entering a new era after 23 years There are days football fans hope will never come. For Portugal, this is one of them. For 23 years, Cristiano Ronaldo has been more than the country’s greatest footballer; he has been its defining sporting figure, a symbol of national pride and constant presence in the lives of supporters. After 234 appearances and 146 goals, the No 7 brought that chapter to a close and on Saturday night the team will play their first game without him . The national side are losing more than a great footballer; they are also losing one of the world’s biggest brands. Daniel Sá, the executive director of the Portuguese institute of marketing administration, believes Portugal require reinvention to attract at least some of the millions of viewers who tuned in because of CR7. item.title: Football Daily | Taking a brief minute to remember Pierre Sage’s impact at Crystal Palace
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! So farewell then, Pierre Sage . Many coaches leave under a cloud, not many have their departures completely obscured by the foul, retch-inducing one emanating from another team’s managerial circus, but such was Sage’s fate . The news section of Crystal Palace’s website helpfully tells you the amount of time it might take you to read each story it links through to. For example it should take four minutes or so to get through Tuesday’s “On this day: five big Crystal Palace birthdays”. “England: I love a knee slide!” will take you five. “Prize draw: be a mascot for our next [Bigger Vase] tie!” is a two-minute job. The statement informing the world of Sage’s exit? One minute. Eighty-three words. By way of illustration, the word “words” was the 84th of this paragraph. Just because the man’s French doesn’t mean his exit should be marked with a shrug. As I have been away at a conference, giving a presentation that the MC described as ‘sobering’, I’ve missed the last few days of football, so I was very sad to read about the passing of the great Danny Kelly . Others are far better placed to give tributes to the great man, but for younger generations who can’t comprehend the football cultural significance, Baker and Kelly represented the peak of football phone-ins. Before it became people ranting and raving about wanting the manager sacked as they’ve lost a few games or wanting the club to spend another few hundred million pounds on yet more players, it was about football supporters and supporting, from fans who actually went to games. Their peak was on BBC Radio in the 1990s, and there are too many examples of their greatness, but if I had to pick one, just one to illustrate it, it would, of course, be Gordon the Dundee United supporter and his bow tie . Rest in Peace, Danny Kelly. You gave us such joy” – Noble Francis. As they no longer seem to be ‘Dr Tottenham’, I was wondering if they had maybe passed the soubriquet on. item.title: Manchester City’s weaknesses under Enzo Maresca are being exposed
item.description: After three straight defeats, City’s manager says he will use the international break to reassess. Their problems may go beyond tactics Sign up for our free newsletter here Enzo Maresca seemed, if not quite baffled by his side’s Saturday defeat to Nottingham Forest, then at least a little put out. After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. The three defeats were all different, Maresca said, although in all of them City had had more possession and more chances. In the 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa two weeks ago, City had 63% of the ball and had 15 chances to Villa’s eight. In the 1-0 home defeat to Brighton last weekend, they had 62% possession and 21 chances to seven. At the City Ground, it was 79% possession and 12 chances to 11. So Maresca is right in one way: City could look at basic statistics and say they had been unfortunate – although Forest could equally point to the fact that they went into that game third top of the expected goals table but second-bottom of the actual table. item.title: That’s a Mora: Rodrigo and Roma rise with Lazio to give Eternal City new life | Nicky Bandini
item.description: Roma and Lazio have both made unbeaten starts to the Serie A season, giving those in the Italian capital dreams of a Scudetto After nine games in 28 days, Gian Piero Gasperini finally got a moment to pause and reflect on Sunday night. The Roma manager was back in Liguria, where he worked for the best part of a decade across two stints at Genoa, to collect an award from Stelle Nello Sport – an association formed to promote sport in the region – celebrating his career achievements and commitment to courageous attacking football. The timing worked out well. Gasperini’s Roma thumped Sassuolo 3-0 on Saturday, bouncing back from a midweek defeat against Manchester United . That result meant the Giallorossi had scored 31 times in 11 Serie A games. In the past 65 years only two Italian teams – the Juventus and Napoli sides of 2017-18 – had made a more prolific start to a top-flight campaign. More importantly, Roma’s victory meant they remained undefeated in domestic competition this season. Just like their neighbours Lazio, who drew 1-1 away against Napoli in the early kick-off on Sunday. Continue reading...

item.title: Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’
item.description: Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.” With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week. Continue reading...

The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. item.title: Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football
item.description: Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it. The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been launched. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most important” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous? Continue reading...

item.title: Billions in revenue proves Fifa right on the World Cup – but only on things it cares about
item.description: The 2026 edition of the tournament brought in untold amounts of money to Gianni Infantino’s governing body The total hasn’t entirely stopped rising yet, still clicking away towards a final tally. Still, Fifa has already announced that it surpassed its own lofty revenue projections for the 2026 World Cup, bringing in $15bn, significantly more than anticipated. It appears that a third of that total – $5bn – came from ticket sales and hospitality alone, per reporting from the Times . That would mean direct income from the matchgoing fans came in five times as high in the United States, Canada and Mexico as it did at the last World Cup, in Qatar in 2022, when the total stood at $929m. While 2026’s expanded World Cup added 40 games to the schedule, the takings nevertheless went from an average of about $14.5m per match to about $48m. Continue reading...

item.title: Choke of the century? Chengdu collapse sets up thrilling Chinese Super League climax
item.description: John Aloisi’s players need a point on the final day to seal their maiden title – but their form has dropped off a cliff With four games of the Chinese Super League to go, Chengdu Rongcheng needed just a point to clinch their first title. With one game to go, they still need a point. What was a formality has become a formidable task. The biggest bottle job in Asian football history is very much on and it would be as popular as it would be dramatic. The coach of the Sichuan club, the former Portsmouth and Coventry striker John Aloisi, has seen a 12-point lead over Dalian Yingbo cut to just three before Sunday’s showdowns. Whatever happens, this is a positive and thrilling end to a season that started negatively – literally – with nine of the 16 top-tier clubs kicking off on minus points. Continue reading...

item.title: Rampant Salford hint that Beckham’s lofty ambitions are not a pipe dream
item.description: The aim of reaching the Championship looks more realistic for a Manchester club in the shadow of City and United After seven seasons in League Two, Salford City are finally threatening to match the hype brought by their high-profile owners. First it was the Class of ’92 who guided them up through the non-league system into the fourth tier but failed to progress any further. Gary Neville and David Beckham remain, part of a new group that took over in May 2025, with this year beginning to look transformational after securing an eighth straight win, against Exeter, to put them five points clear at the top. The budget has increased, allowing the club to sign a number of players who will feel they are above League Two standard. Striker Macaulay Langstaff arrived from Millwall; the last time he played at this level, he scored 28 league goals in a season for Notts County. Match-winner Will Aimson spent the past two seasons in the division above with Wigan and has dropped down because of Salford’s project. Continue reading...

item.description: Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League I felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. item.title: A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?
item.description: It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them. And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings. item.title: Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe
item.description: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points José Mourinho had already done the por qu é? , the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out. Continue reading...

item.title: Ian Holloway’s circus: why the manager’s antics are no laughing matter for fans
item.description: Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.” To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
